blocks.content: 1. FIRST UNDERSTAND THIS — WHY CLAUSES MATTER

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: A clause is built on the fundamental distinction between complete thoughts (independent) and incomplete thoughts (dependent).
The three major clauses heavily tested in competitive exams are Noun Clauses, Adjective Clauses, and Adverb Clauses.
Noun clauses function as 'things' (subjects or objects) and are prone to word-order errors with question words.
Adjective clauses describe nouns using relative pronouns and relative adverbs, divided into defining and non-defining types.
Adverb clauses supply extra information and frequently trap candidates with future tense misuse and double conjunctions.
Advanced areas like conditional clauses, subjunctive mood, participle clauses, and reduced clauses require precise logical analysis.

19. SUBJUNCTIVE — WHY ‘WERE’ IS USED

items: Question Word Order Error: Noun clauses in assertive sentences must use normal statement order (Subject + Verb), not inverted question word order.
Future Tense Trap: Avoid using future tense verbs (will/shall) inside time and conditional adverb clauses.
Double Conjunction Error: Never use redundant conjunctions (e.g., combining 'Although' with 'But') to connect two clauses.
Subjunctive 'Were': Use 'were' instead of 'was' in imaginary conditional clauses regardless of subject number.
